scenes.say: Vidya Pramaan. One student, one APAAR ID, one verifiable record. This is our working prototype for Smart India Hackathon problem statement S I H, 2 6 2 6 3, by Team AI Riders.

scenes.text: AICTE approves the intake of every programme, but today it receives only total enrolment, and late. An excess seat costs five times the fee. In one Supreme Court case, forty-two excess seats meant a fine of twenty-three crore rupees. Vidya Pramaan checks every admission against the approved intake, student by student, keyed on APAAR.
Everything you will see is the working prototype, on synthetic data. It has seven roles. We start as a college admission office.
The home screen shows every programme with its approved intake. B.Tech Computer Science has sixty approved seats, and none are filled yet.

The college uploads its admission list, as Excel, as CSV, or through its ERP system's API. All seventy-seven rows are checked against thirty-one explained rules and the APAAR registry, in a fraction of a second. Sixty-five rows can be accepted. Twelve come back to the college.

Each returned row says why, in plain language. An APAAR ID that is missing, invalid, or not in the registry. A foreign national without a passport number. And seat sixty-one of sixty: an admission beyond the approved intake, stopped at upload instead of found later in an inspection.

Warnings do not block a row. A name that differs from the registry, or a student already enrolled at another college, goes to AICTE for review. And a student who opted out of APAAR gets a provisional ID and is never rejected for it.
The college submits. Sixty-five records are stored, and the seat ledger reads sixty of sixty. Never sixty-one.

At AICTE, the national view refreshes after every submission. A scan across all institutions looks for duplicate students, intake breaches and shared contacts. Each college gets a risk score against its peers, with the reasons spelled out.
Open any college to see why it was ranked: which measures differ from its peer group, and by how much. A score only decides what to review first. It never decides the outcome.

Here, one APAAR ID is active at two colleges at the same time. The officer sees both records side by side and decides, with a written reason. That decision is remembered, so the same case is never raised again.
This case has no shared APAAR ID at all. The matcher is built for Indian names. Mohd and Mohammed match, initials are handled, but twins born on the same day are kept apart.

scenes.text: And this is a ghost-admission ring. One phone number sits behind eight students at two colleges, a pattern no single college could see.

Every action goes into a hash-chained audit trail, sealed with signed checkpoints. Even if someone with database access rewrites the whole history and recomputes every hash, the check fails, as you see here.
Universities receive the APAAR ID and student ID of every student in their affiliated colleges, ready to print on degrees with a verification QR.
Now an employer wants to verify a candidate. It sends a consent request, and chooses only the facts it needs.
The student sees the request, with who is asking and why, and approves it with a one-time password. Every access is logged in the student's own history.
The employer sees only the fields the student approved. Everything else stays hidden.
Anyone can scan the certificate QR. The signature is checked on the phone itself, together with a signed revocation list, so it works even offline.
Change a single character in the certificate, and verification fails.
The portal installs as an app on a phone, and has a Hindi option.

To be clear about what is real. The upload, rules, national scan, risk scores, consent, signed QR and audit trail are built, and covered by sixty-five automated tests. The APAAR registry and DigiLocker are simulated until partner access is granted. All accuracy figures come from synthetic data, and a pilot with fifty colleges will measure the real ones.
Vidya Pramaan. One student, one APAAR ID, one verifiable record. Try it yourself at the link on screen. Thank you.
